cards.lead: Earthen mound complexes in the Lower Mississippi Valley
cards.note: The dates hold: sources date the first earthworks at Watson Brake to about 3500 BCE and substantial mound-raising to about 3350 BCE. No opened source says the mounds were independent of other traditions, so origin is set to unknown.
cards.name: Watson Brake mound complex, Louisiana
cards.summary: Hunter-gatherers at Watson Brake, Louisiana, raised one of the earliest known earthen mound complexes in North America, about 3500 BCE.
cards.description: Watson Brake in northeast Louisiana is the largest and most complex of the Middle Archaic earthen mound complexes of the lower Mississippi valley, which the 2005 full report by Saunders and colleagues calls remote antecedents of the much younger Poverty Point earthworks. Minor earthworks were begun there at about 3500 BCE and substantial mound-raising at about 3350 BCE, continuing in stages after 3000 BCE.
cards.origin_note: The sources date Watson Brake to the Middle Archaic and describe a local sequence of sites, but none says whether the builders knew of earlier mounds elsewhere, so independence is not established.

impact.note: Lead scores kept: a regional achievement whose later mound tradition is not yet shown here.

events.label: c. 3500 BCE
events.statement: Minor earthworks were begun at Watson Brake at about 3500 BCE, dated by radiocarbon and luminescence.
events.quote: Very extensive coring and stratigraphic studies, aided by 25 radiocarbon dates and six luminescence dates, show that minor earthworks were begun here at ca. 3500 B.C.

events.label: c. 3350 to 3000 BCE
events.statement: Substantial mound-raising began at about 3350 BCE and continued in stages until some time after 3000 BCE.
events.quote: Substantial moundraising began ca. 3350 B.C. and continued in stages until some time after 3000

cards.lead: Monumental platforms and pyramids in Formative Mesoamerica
cards.note: The lead's c. 1400 to 800 BCE does not fit the sources for this site: the Nature paper dates the Aguada Fénix plateau to 1000 to 800 BC. The Olmec plateau at San Lorenzo is older, but the same paper says it has no pyramids and gives its heyday as 1400 to 1150 BC.
cards.name: Aguada Fénix plateau, Tabasco
cards.summary: A 1,400-metre artificial plateau at Aguada Fénix, Tabasco, is the oldest monumental construction found in the Maya area, built about 1000 to 800 BCE.
cards.description: Inomata and colleagues used lidar and excavation to identify Aguada Fénix, an artificial plateau 1,400 metres long and 10 to 15 metres high with nine causeways. Bayesian analysis of 69 radiocarbon dates places its construction between 1000 and 800 BC. The authors call it the oldest monumental construction in the Maya area and the largest in the region's pre-Hispanic history, and they note its similarities to the earlier Olmec centre of San Lorenzo.
cards.origin_note: The paper compares Aguada Fénix with San Lorenzo and raises the question of Olmec influence on the Maya lowlands, so independence is not established.

impact.note: Reach lowered from the lead's 2: the sources tie the plateau to the Maya lowlands, and its later spread is not shown here.

events.label: c. 1000 to 800 BCE
events.statement: Bayesian analysis of 69 radiocarbon dates places the construction of the Aguada Fénix plateau between 1000 and 800 BC.
events.quote: We dated this construction to between 1000 and 800 bc using a Bayesian analysis of radiocarbon dates.

sources.title: Monumental architecture at Aguada Fénix and the rise of Maya civilization

open_questions: Coordinates were taken from the Wikipedia infobox, which is not a cited source.
The earliest large platforms at San Lorenzo and La Venta need their own dated records; the lead's pyramid claims were not verified.
The Maya corbelled vault and burnt-lime stucco records suggested by the lead were not researched.

cards.lead: Stone temple platforms in East Polynesia
cards.note: The lead's c. 1200 to 1600 CE does not fit the cited dating for Society Islands temples: the coral-faced ahu on Mo'orea were built in about AD 1620 to 1760, and the Rapa Nui and Hawaiian claims were not verified.
cards.name: Coral-faced ahu temple platforms, Mo'orea, Society Islands
cards.summary: Chiefly temple platforms on Mo'orea were elaborated rapidly, in about 140 years before European contact, with coral and cut-stone facings.
cards.description: Sharp and Kahn dated coral used as architectural elements in 22 marae on Mo'orea by uranium-thorium methods. The three largest coastal marae and 19 inland marae show that temple architecture developed rapidly, from low ahu faced with Acropora fan corals to stepped platforms of cut Porites blocks. Chiefly lineages used these temples to assert power, and the largest coastal ones were built shortly before first European contact in AD 1767.
cards.origin_note: The paper treats Mo'orea's temple development as a local sequence, and does not say whether it was independent of other Polynesian temple traditions.

impact.note: Lead scores kept: a regional chiefly temple tradition, with no evidence here of wider spread.

events.label: c. AD 1620 to 1760
events.statement: Uranium-thorium dates on coral architecture show temple building on Mo'orea developed over about 140 years, from about AD 1620 to 1760.
events.quote: The dates indicate that temple architecture on Mo‘orea Island developed rapidly over a period of approximately 140 y ( ca. AD 1620–1760)

sources.title: Rapid evolution of ritual architecture in central Polynesia indicated by precise 230Th/U coral dating
sources.publisher: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 107(30)

open_questions: Kahn (cited in the paper) argues that simple platform marae without ahu were built about AD 1430 to 1530; this earlier phase needs its own check.
The Rapa Nui ahu chronology (a 2020 Bayesian study by DiNapoli and colleagues that places early ahu between the early 14th and mid-15th centuries AD) was seen only in search results and not opened.
Hawaiian heiau dating and the moving and raising of stone were not researched.

cards.note: The Home Insurance Building (1885) is not a steel skeleton and was not the first skyscraper: only three floors had steel beams, and the rest of its metal frame was iron with masonry walls. The lead's first_known origin fails, so origin is set to unknown.
cards.name: Home Insurance Building, Chicago
cards.summary: Chicago's Home Insurance Building, completed in 1885, is often credited as the first skyscraper, but its frame was mostly iron, not steel.
cards.description: The Home Insurance Building was completed in Chicago in 1885 by William Le Baron Jenney. Barr's 2024 analysis argues that the building was neither the first skyscraper nor the first steel skeleton, and that most of its metal frame was wrought or cast iron with masonry walls. The 'first skyscraper' claim was promoted by Jenney and Chicago boosters from the mid-1890s, and the myth was repeated in a 1931 trustees' report.
cards.origin_note: Iron framing predates this building (the Ditherington mill in England is dated 1797 by the ICE page, not cited here), and no source establishes whether Chicago's frame derived from it.

impact.note: Lowered from the lead's reach 3 and generativity 2: the building is not the first steel skeleton, so its own descent is narrower than the concept's.

events.statement: The Home Insurance Building was completed in Chicago in 1885, a building later called the first skyscraper.
events.quote: with his Home Insurance Building (HIB), completed in Chicago in 1885

sources.title: Revisiting Jenney and the first skyscraper (working paper)

open_questions: The first fully steel-framed Chicago buildings (1889 to 1890) need their own records.
Ditherington flax mill (1797), an internal iron frame, should be checked as a separate record.
The Barr paper is a working paper, not peer-reviewed; a published version should be checked.

cards.lead: Water-storage dams in the Early Bronze Age Levant and Egypt
cards.note: The lead's c. 3000 to 2600 BCE does not fit the Jawa dam: the sources give a range of 3630 to 3090 cal. BC and call the dam about 3600 BC. The Egyptian Sadd el-Kafara was not verified from an opened source.
cards.name: Jawa dam, Wadi Rajil, Jordan
cards.summary: The Jawa dam in the Jordanian basalt desert is described as the most ancient known dam, dated to about 3600 BCE.
cards.description: Müller-Neuhof's 2019 review of the Jawa Hinterland Project describes a dam at Jawa, Wadi Rajil, as appearing to be the most ancient dam in the world, dated to about 3600 BC. Radiocarbon dates from the early occupation phase at Jawa and from the dam range from 3630 to 3090 cal. BC, with dwelling horizons concentrated between 3500 and 3400 cal. BC. The paper describes Jawa as characterized by extensive waterworks.
cards.origin_note: The source says the dam 'appears to be the most ancient dam in the world' on present evidence, a first-known claim that later finds could overturn.

impact.note: Lead scores kept: the water-storage effect on one settlement, with a later regional dam tradition not shown here.

cards.lead: Aqueduct water supply in the Aztec Basin of Mexico
cards.note: The lead's c. 1420s does not match the INAH marker, which dates the aqueduct designed by Nezahualcoyotl to 1466. Other dates in search results (1418, 1454 to 1466) were not verified from opened sources, and the twin-channel masonry claim was not checked. Origin is set to unknown.
cards.name: Chapultepec aqueduct, Tenochtitlan
cards.summary: An aqueduct designed by Nezahualcoyotl brought Chapultepec spring water to Tenochtitlan from 1466, according to an INAH marker.
cards.description: The INAH marker at Chapultepec hill says the springs began to be used during the government of Moctezuma Ilhuicamina, thanks to an aqueduct designed by Nezahualcoyotl in 1466. Water was collected in tanks from three springs and carried to the city, and the marker records that the line later ran along what is now Melchor Ocampo Road. Its date for the Aztec aqueduct is the one this card rests on.
cards.origin_note: The marker describes the aqueduct as designed in 1466 but does not say whether it had earlier models, so independence is not established.

impact.note: Depth lowered from the lead's 2: the marker describes an improved supply to existing spring tanks rather than a new capability.

events.statement: According to the INAH marker, the springs began to be used through an aqueduct designed by Nezahualcoyotl in 1466.
events.quote: The springs began to be used during the government of Moctezuma Ilhuicamina thanks to an aqueduct designed by Nezahualcyotl in 1466.

sources.title: Manantiales y Cajas de Agua / Springs and Water Tanks (INAH historical marker)
sources.publisher: Instituto Nacional de Antropología e Historia (INAH) marker, Historical Marker Database

open_questions: Archaeological and Spanish-language sources need to settle the date (1418, 1454 to 1466 and 1466 all appear in search results).
Nezahualcoyotl's dike (1449) and the Tetzcotzinco works were not researched.
Earlier Mesoamerican water channels (Palenque, Teotihuacan, Monte Alban) need their own records.
The lead's Assyrian Jerwan record (c. 690 BCE) is a separate first-known search for the aqueduct concept.
